title: Tahmid English Curriculum Level 1–32: educator audit
reviewScope: All 480 learning items, including English, Japanese, examples/dialogues, usage and pronunciation guidance. Image metadata is tracked separately in the asset attribution ledger.
criteria: Everyday usefulness and frequency within topic
Unique learning purpose and meaningful recycling
Stable IDs and existing progress/access preservation

exampleSentence.before: This book is new.

exampleJapanese.before: この本は新しいです。
exampleJapanese.after: これは私の本です。

exampleSentence.before: May I use your pen?

exampleJapanese.before: あなたのペンを使ってもいいですか。
exampleJapanese.after: 私はペンを持っています。

exampleSentence.before: My desk is by the window.

exampleJapanese.before: 私の机は窓のそばです。
exampleJapanese.after: これは私の机です。

exampleSentence.before: Please sit on this chair.

exampleJapanese.before: この椅子に座ってください。
exampleJapanese.after: 椅子に座ってください。

exampleSentence.before: My bag is under the desk.

exampleJapanese.before: 私のかばんは机の下です。
exampleJapanese.after: これは私のかばんです。

exampleSentence.before: Our teacher is kind.

exampleJapanese.before: 私たちの先生は親切です。
exampleJapanese.after: こちらは私の先生です。

exampleSentence.before: Every student has a notebook.

exampleJapanese.before: 生徒はみんなノートを持っています。
exampleJapanese.after: 私は生徒です。

exampleSentence.before: The lesson starts at ten.

exampleJapanese.before: 授業は10時に始まります。
exampleJapanese.after: 今からレッスンが始まります。

exampleSentence.before: We saw a green bird.

exampleJapanese.before: 私たちは緑の鳥を見ました。
exampleJapanese.after: かばんは緑色です。

exampleSentence.before: He wears a black hat.

exampleJapanese.before: 彼は黒い帽子をかぶっています。
exampleJapanese.after: これは黒いペンです。

exampleSentence.before: Draw a circle around the answer.

exampleJapanese.before: 答えを丸で囲んでください。
exampleJapanese.after: 丸を描いてください。

pronunciationHint.before: Open with /st/ and hold the central vowel.
pronunciationHint.after: Join /s/ and /t/. US English ends with an r sound; the usual UK model has a long vowel without r.

exampleSentence.before: Stand in a straight line.

exampleJapanese.before: まっすぐ一列に並んでください。
exampleJapanese.after: まっすぐな線を描いてください。

commonMistake.before: Do not pronounce it like “lean.”
commonMistake.after: For the shape, say “draw a line.” “Stand in line” uses the separate meaning of a queue.

exampleSentence.before: My grandmother tells funny stories.

exampleJapanese.before: 私の祖母は面白い話をしてくれます。
exampleJapanese.after: 私の祖母は親切です。

exampleSentence.before: His grandfather grows tomatoes.

exampleJapanese.before: 彼の祖父はトマトを育てています。
exampleJapanese.after: 私の祖父は本が好きです。

exampleSentence.before: Put the hat on your head.

exampleJapanese.before: 帽子を頭にかぶってください。
exampleJapanese.after: 頭を触ってください。

exampleSentence.before: Wash your face with warm water.

exampleJapanese.before: ぬるま湯で顔を洗ってください。
exampleJapanese.after: 顔を洗ってください。

pronunciationHint.before: Begin with /ɪ/ and glide gently toward r.
pronunciationHint.after: Start with a relaxed /ɪ/. US English ends in r; the usual UK model does not pronounce a final r here.

exampleSentence.before: Raise your hand if you know.

exampleJapanese.before: 分かったら手を挙げてください。
exampleJapanese.after: 手を挙げてください。

exampleSentence.before: She carried the box in one arm.

exampleJapanese.before: 彼女は片腕で箱を運びました。
exampleJapanese.after: 右腕を上げてください。

exampleSentence.before: Stretch each leg slowly.

exampleJapanese.before: 両脚をゆっくり伸ばしてください。
exampleJapanese.after: 左脚が痛いです。

exampleSentence.before: I made toast with this bread.

exampleJapanese.before: このパンでトーストを作りました。
exampleJapanese.after: 私はパンが好きです。

exampleSentence.before: Would you like an egg?

exampleJapanese.before: 卵はいかがですか。
exampleJapanese.after: 私は卵を1つ持っています。

exampleSentence.before: Please put the milk in the fridge.

exampleJapanese.before: 牛乳を冷蔵庫に入れてください。
exampleJapanese.after: 私は牛乳を飲みます。

exampleSentence.before: I cut the apple in half.

exampleJapanese.before: りんごを半分に切りました。
exampleJapanese.after: このりんごは緑色です。

exampleSentence.before: We had chicken for lunch.

exampleJapanese.before: 昼食に鶏肉を食べました。
exampleJapanese.after: 私は鶏肉とご飯が好きです。

commonMistake.before: Use “chicken” without “a” when you mean the food.
commonMistake.after: The food is uncountable: “some chicken.” “A chicken” means one bird.

exampleSentence.before: The soup smells wonderful.

exampleJapanese.before: そのスープはとてもいい香りです。
exampleJapanese.after: スープは熱いです。

exampleSentence.before: Their house has a small garden.

exampleJapanese.before: 彼らの家には小さな庭があります。
exampleJapanese.after: 私たちの家は小さいです。

pronunciationHint.after: A long /uː/ is common. Some speakers use a shorter /ʊ/; follow the voice you are practising.

exampleSentence.before: My room is upstairs.

exampleJapanese.before: 私の部屋は2階です。
exampleJapanese.after: 私の部屋はきれいです。

exampleSentence.before: The bedroom gets morning sun.

exampleJapanese.before: 寝室には朝日が入ります。
exampleJapanese.after: ここは私の寝室です。

exampleSentence.before: I went to bed early.
exampleSentence.after: My bed is next to the window.

exampleJapanese.before: 私は早く寝ました。
exampleJapanese.after: 私のベッドは窓の隣にあります。

commonMistake.before: “Key” and “quay” can sound the same, but meanings differ.
commonMistake.after: A key opens a lock. Use “my key” for one, and “my keys” for several.

exampleSentence.before: The clock is five minutes fast.
exampleSentence.after: The clock is on the wall.

exampleJapanese.before: その時計は5分進んでいます。
exampleJapanese.after: 時計は壁にあります。

exampleSentence.before: The horse ran across the field.

exampleJapanese.before: 馬は野原を走りました。
exampleJapanese.after: 馬は速く走れます。

exampleSentence.before: The pig rolled in the mud.

exampleJapanese.before: 豚は泥の中を転がりました。
exampleJapanese.after: 豚はピンク色です。

pronunciationHint.before: Stress LI and make the ending two light sounds.
pronunciationHint.after: Stress the first syllable: LI-on. Let the second syllable stay light.

exampleSentence.before: The lion rested in the shade.

exampleJapanese.before: ライオンは日陰で休みました。
exampleJapanese.after: ライオンは大きいです。

exampleSentence.before: An elephant can use its trunk like a hand.

exampleJapanese.before: 象は鼻を手のように使えます。
exampleJapanese.after: 象は耳が大きいです。

exampleSentence.before: I run around the park each morning.

exampleJapanese.before: 私は毎朝公園を走ります。
exampleJapanese.after: 私は速く走れます。

commonMistake.before: “Sit” is intransitive; do not use it as “seat someone.”
commonMistake.after: Say “sit on a chair” or “sit down.” “Seat” is a different verb: “Please seat the guests.”

exampleSentence.before: Stand near the yellow sign.

exampleJapanese.before: 黄色い標識の近くに立ってください。
exampleJapanese.after: 立ってください。

exampleSentence.before: Open the box carefully.

exampleJapanese.before: 箱を注意して開けてください。
exampleJapanese.after: 本を開いてください。

exampleSentence.before: Close the gate behind you.

exampleJapanese.before: 後ろの門を閉めてください。
exampleJapanese.after: ドアを閉めてください。

exampleSentence.before: Listen to the whole sentence.

exampleJapanese.before: 文全体を聞いてください。
exampleJapanese.after: 先生の話を聞いてください。

pronunciationHint.before: Usually one smooth syllable in natural speech.
pronunciationHint.after: US English often has one smooth syllable /taɪrd/. UK English may glide through /aɪə/ before d.

exampleSentence.before: He was angry about the broken promise.
exampleSentence.after: He is angry about the broken toy.

exampleJapanese.before: 彼は約束が破られたことに怒っていました。
exampleJapanese.after: 彼はおもちゃが壊れたことに怒っています。

pronunciationHint.before: Stress HUN and pronounce ng as one sound.

commonMistake.before: “Pants” is plural in form: say “these pants.”
commonMistake.after: US “pants” means trousers; UK “pants” usually means underwear. For this item, practise the US clothing meaning: “these pants.”

commonMistake.before: Say “a ticket to Tokyo,” not “a ticket for Tokyo” when naming a destination.
commonMistake.after: Use “a ticket to Tokyo” for the destination, and “a ticket for the ten o’clock train” for a particular service.

commonMistake.before: Use “clean” without “up” when removing dirt generally.
commonMistake.after: “Clean the kitchen” focuses on making it clean. “Clean up the kitchen” can also include tidying it.

commonMistake.before: Do not use “bring” when the direction is away from the speaker.
commonMistake.after: “Carry” describes holding and moving something. “Bring” and “take” also tell us about the direction of movement.

commonMistake.before: Use “fix” for repair, not every kind of problem-solving in formal writing.
commonMistake.after: Use “fix” directly with the problem or broken object: “fix the handle,” not “fix to the handle.”

commonMistake.before: Say “pack a bag,” not “pack up a bag” unless emphasizing completion.
commonMistake.after: “Pack a bag” means put things in it. “Pack up” can mean collect your things before leaving.

commonMistake.before: Use “ask someone a question,” not “ask a question to someone.”
commonMistake.after: The useful everyday pattern is “ask someone a question.” Use “ask for help” when you want assistance.

commonMistake.before: Do not add “again” unless repetition needs extra emphasis.
commonMistake.after: Say “repeat the word,” not “repeat to the word.” “Repeat it again” is possible when another repetition is needed.

commonMistake.before: Use “invite someone to an event,” not “invite someone for an event.”
commonMistake.after: Use “invite someone to a party.” With a meal, both “invite someone to dinner” and “invite someone for dinner” occur.

exampleSentence.before: I finished my homework before dinner.
exampleSentence.after: I put off my homework until the last minute.

exampleJapanese.before: 夕食前に宿題を終えました。
exampleJapanese.after: 私はぎりぎりまで宿題を後回しにしました。

exampleSentence.before: Write one question about the story.
exampleSentence.after: Ask a follow-up question if the answer is unclear.

exampleJapanese.before: 物語について質問を1つ書いてください。
exampleJapanese.after: 答えがはっきりしなければ、追加で質問してください。

exampleSentence.before: I keep new vocabulary in a notebook.
exampleSentence.after: I keep track of new words in a notebook.

exampleJapanese.before: 新しい単語をノートに書いています。
exampleJapanese.after: 私は新しい単語をノートに記録しています。

exampleSentence.before: Check the word in a learner’s dictionary.
exampleSentence.after: Look the word up in a dictionary, then make your own sentence.

exampleJapanese.before: 学習者向け辞書でその単語を調べてください。
exampleJapanese.after: 辞書でその単語を調べてから、自分で文を作ってください。

exampleSentence.before: Science is my favorite subject.
exampleSentence.after: Which subject would you like to get better at?

exampleJapanese.before: 理科は私の好きな科目です。
exampleJapanese.after: どの科目がもっと得意になりたいですか。

exampleSentence.before: Our office is near the station.
exampleSentence.after: I work from home twice a week and spend the other days at the office.

exampleJapanese.before: 私たちのオフィスは駅の近くです。
exampleJapanese.after: 週に2日は在宅で働き、ほかの日はオフィスで働きます。

commonMistake.before: Say “report on a topic,” not “report about” in formal contexts.
commonMistake.after: Use “write a report on the results.” As a verb, “report to the manager” identifies the person you report to.

pronunciationHint.before: Stress COL and hold /iː/ at the end.
pronunciationHint.after: Stress COL, then use /iː/ and finish with /ɡ/.

commonMistake.before: Do not use “colleague” for every friend at work unless you work together.
commonMistake.after: A colleague is someone you work with; “classmate” is someone in your class.

pronunciationHint.after: Stress MED. Speakers may use two syllables or a light middle syllable; do not stress the ending.

exampleSentence.before: Each guest received a name card.
exampleSentence.after: We introduced each guest by name so nobody felt left out.

exampleJapanese.before: 客は一人ずつ名札を受け取りました。
exampleJapanese.after: 誰も取り残されたと感じないように、一人ずつ名前でお客さんを紹介しました。

exampleSentence.before: Practice the dialogue with a partner.
exampleSentence.after: Check with your partner before making the final decision.

exampleJapanese.before: 相手と会話を練習してください。
exampleJapanese.after: 最終的な決定をする前に、一緒に取り組む相手に確認してください。

commonMistake.before: Use “trust someone,” not “trust in someone,” for ordinary confidence.
commonMistake.after: “Trust someone” is the direct everyday pattern. “Trust in someone” can express strong faith and is also correct.

pronunciationHint.before: As a noun, stress SPECT strongly.
pronunciationHint.after: Stress SPECT in both the noun and the verb.

commonMistake.before: Something is convenient for a person, not convenient to a person.
commonMistake.after: Say “The time is convenient for me.” To describe your own availability, say “I’m free,” not “I’m convenient.”

commonMistake.before: Say “It is possible to…,” not “It is possible that I can…” when simpler.
commonMistake.after: Use “It is possible to change it.” For personal ability, use “I can change it,” not “I am possible to change it.”

japanese.after: 確信している・確かな

commonMistake.before: Do not confuse adjective “patient” with noun “patient.”
commonMistake.after: As an adjective, say “be patient with someone.” “A patient” is a different meaning: a person receiving medical care.

exampleSentence.before: Be careful with the hot plate.
exampleSentence.after: Be careful not to share the wrong file.

exampleJapanese.before: 熱い皿に気をつけてください。
exampleJapanese.after: 間違ったファイルを共有しないように気をつけてください。

exampleSentence.before: Choose a unique password for this account.
exampleSentence.after: I forgot my password and had to reset it.

exampleJapanese.before: このアカウントには固有のパスワードを選んでください。
exampleJapanese.after: パスワードを忘れたので、再設定しなければなりませんでした。

commonMistake.before: Do not share or reuse passwords.
commonMistake.after: “Reset a password” means choose a new one after losing access. “Forget” describes what happened to your memory.

commonMistake.before: Not every material marked plastic is locally recyclable.
commonMistake.after: Use “recycle paper” directly. “Recyclable” describes a material; “recycling” names the process.

commonMistake.before: “Reduce” is transitive; say what becomes smaller.
commonMistake.after: “Reduce water use” names what you make smaller. “Reduce by ten percent” gives the amount of the change.

pronunciationHint.before: Stress RE in US English; UK stress may differ.
pronunciationHint.after: Stress differs across speakers and varieties. Listen for the stressed syllable in your selected US or UK model.

commonMistake.before: Say “relieved to know” or “relieved that…,” not “relieved about” in every case.
commonMistake.after: Use “relieved to hear the news” or “relieved that everyone is safe.” “Relieved about” also works with an appropriate noun.

pronunciationHint.before: The l is silent; hold the vowel.
pronunciationHint.after: A pronunciation without /l/ is common in both models. Some speakers pronounce a light /l/.

commonMistake.before: Do not pronounce the written l.
commonMistake.after: “Stay calm” describes your state. Use “calmly” with an action: “speak calmly.”

commonMistake.before: Compare A with B to examine differences; “compare to” often notes similarity.
commonMistake.after: “Compare A with B” and “compare A to B” can both introduce a comparison; explain which similarities or differences you mean.

pronunciationHint.before: As a verb, stress TRAST; noun stress often begins earlier.
pronunciationHint.after: As a verb, stress TRAST. The noun usually stresses CON.

commonMistake.before: Say “within budget” or “over budget,” not “inside the budget.”
commonMistake.after: Use “stay within budget” for keeping to a spending limit, and “go over budget” for spending too much.

exampleSentence.before: Your luggage can go under the seat.
exampleSentence.after: Could you tell me where to report missing luggage?

exampleJapanese.before: 荷物は座席の下に置けます。
exampleJapanese.after: 荷物が届かない場合、どこに届け出ればよいか教えていただけますか。

exampleSentence.before: Keep your passport in a safe place.
exampleSentence.after: I had to renew my passport before I could book the trip.

exampleJapanese.before: パスポートを安全な場所に保管してください。
exampleJapanese.after: 旅行を予約する前に、パスポートを更新する必要がありました。

commonMistake.before: Do not drop the final t.
commonMistake.after: Use “renew a passport” when you need a new period of validity. “Update” usually describes changing information.

exampleSentence.before: We went through customs quickly.
exampleSentence.after: We were asked to declare the food we were carrying at customs.

exampleJapanese.before: 私たちはすぐに税関を通過しました。
exampleJapanese.after: 税関で、持っていた食品を申告するよう求められました。

exampleSentence.before: Kyoto is our final destination.
exampleSentence.after: We changed our destination after the original flight was canceled.

exampleJapanese.before: 京都が私たちの最終目的地です。
exampleJapanese.after: 最初の便が欠航したので、私たちは目的地を変更しました。

exampleSentence.before: The price includes accommodation and breakfast.
exampleSentence.after: We need to arrange accommodation within walking distance of the station.

exampleJapanese.before: 料金には宿泊と朝食が含まれています。
exampleJapanese.after: 駅から歩ける範囲で宿泊先を手配する必要があります。

exampleSentence.before: I changed the reservation online.
exampleSentence.after: Could you confirm whether my reservation includes breakfast?

exampleJapanese.before: オンラインで予約を変更しました。
exampleJapanese.after: 私の予約に朝食が含まれるか確認していただけますか。

exampleSentence.before: Check the departure time on the board.
exampleSentence.after: Our departure was brought forward, so we had to leave the hotel earlier.

exampleJapanese.before: 掲示板で出発時刻を確認してください。
exampleJapanese.after: 出発時刻が早まったので、ホテルをもっと早く出なければなりませんでした。

exampleSentence.before: Please wait in the arrival hall.
exampleSentence.after: Please let the hotel know your estimated time of arrival.

exampleJapanese.before: 到着ロビーで待ってください。
exampleJapanese.after: 到着予定時刻をホテルに知らせてください。

commonMistake.before: Use “on arrival” for the moment you reach a place.
commonMistake.after: “On arrival” means when you reach a place. At an airport, the usual sign is “Arrivals,” and the room is the “arrivals hall.”

exampleSentence.before: The train leaves from platform six.
exampleSentence.after: The platform changed at the last minute, and we nearly missed the train.

exampleJapanese.before: 電車は6番ホームから出ます。
exampleJapanese.after: 直前にホームが変更になり、もう少しで電車に乗り遅れるところでした。

exampleSentence.before: We have a short transfer in Seoul.
exampleSentence.after: We missed our connection because the airport transfer took longer than expected.

exampleJapanese.before: ソウルで短い乗り継ぎがあります。
exampleJapanese.after: 空港間の移動が予想以上にかかり、乗り継ぎ便に間に合いませんでした。

commonMistake.before: Stress changes between common noun and verb uses.
commonMistake.after: An airport transfer is transport between an airport and another place. A connection is the next flight or train you catch.

exampleSentence.before: I prefer tea without sugar.
exampleSentence.after: I'd prefer to wait until we have all the details.

exampleJapanese.before: 私は砂糖なしの紅茶のほうが好きです。
exampleJapanese.after: 詳細がすべて分かるまで待ちたいです。

exampleSentence.before: Rain is likely this evening.
exampleSentence.after: We're likely to miss the deadline unless we get more help.

exampleJapanese.before: 今晩は雨が降りそうです。
exampleJapanese.after: もっと協力を得られなければ、締め切りに間に合いそうにありません。

commonMistake.before: Say “It is likely that…” or “is likely to…,” not “maybe likely.”
commonMistake.after: Use “be likely to do” or “It is likely that…”; do not say “I likely go” when you mean “I am likely to go.”

exampleSentence.before: The shop is unlikely to open today.
exampleSentence.after: The plan is unlikely to work without a reliable backup.

exampleJapanese.before: その店は今日開かないでしょう。
exampleJapanese.after: 確実な代替策がなければ、この計画はうまくいきそうにありません。

commonMistake.before: Use “persuade someone to do”; “convince” commonly takes “that.”
commonMistake.after: Use “persuade someone to do something.” “Convince someone to do something” is also common, especially in US English.

pronunciationHint.after: Stress the second syllable /ˈnɒl/ (UK) or /ˈnɑːl/ (US). Finish with /ɪdʒ/.

commonMistake.before: The initial k is pronounced; the written w is not separately heard.
commonMistake.after: The k in “ack” is pronounced, but the written w is silent.

exampleSentence.before: Please respond by the end of the week.
exampleSentence.after: How we respond to criticism can be just as important as the work itself.

exampleJapanese.before: 週末までに返答してください。
exampleJapanese.after: 批判にどう応じるかは、仕事そのものと同じくらい大切なことがあります。

commonMistake.before: Help me please. も通じますが、Please help me. は初級者にも使いやすい形です。
commonMistake.after: Please help me. と Help me, please. はどちらも自然です。困っていることを穏やかな声で伝えましょう。

commonMistake.before: I like this it. のように one と it を重ねません。
commonMistake.after: this one は一つの物を指します。I like this one it. のように one と it を重ねません。

items.title: I don't like it very much.

commonMistake.before: Can I have a water? より、量を表す some water が基本です。
commonMistake.after: 基本は some water です。店で a water と言うと、水を一杯・一本注文する意味で自然に使えます。

items.title: Could I get this without cheese?
Do you have this in blue?
How do I get to the station?

commonMistake.before: How can I go the station? ではなく、get to the station が自然です。
commonMistake.after: get to the station と、行き先の前に to を入れます。How can I get to the station? も自然です。

items.title: What are you doing this weekend?
I need to take a break.

commonMistake.before: Do you feel better? も正しいですが、回復中の様子には Are you feeling better? が自然です。
commonMistake.after: Are you feeling better? と Do you feel better? はどちらも回復を気づかう自然な質問です。better は good / well の比較級です。

items.title: Do you want to join us?

commonMistake.before: Next time maybe. より Maybe next time. の語順が自然です。
commonMistake.after: Maybe next time. は確約ではありません。本当に次の予定を立てたいなら、別の日を提案しましょう。

naturalUsage.before: クラスメートを共同作業に誘う簡潔な表現です。
naturalUsage.after: 先生には一緒に作業してよいかを尋ねられます。友達には協力を提案する形にもなります。

commonMistake.before: work together with us のように不要な語を足さず、二人ならこの形で十分です。
commonMistake.after: Can we work together? では work の原形を使います。working を続けません。

items.title: I left my notebook at home.

commonMistake.before: I forgot my notebook at home. より left my notebook at home が自然です。
commonMistake.after: I left my notebook at home. は置いてきた場所を伝えます。I forgot my notebook. は持参し忘れたことに焦点を当てます。

items.title: It was better than I expected.

naturalUsage.before: 確定に近い個人的な計画を plan to で伝えます。
naturalUsage.after: plan to で今考えている計画を伝えます。予定が確定しているとは限りません。

items.title: Which platform does it leave from?

situation.before: 近所の店や観光地を教えてもらうとき
situation.after: 食事をする場所など、目的を伝えてから近くのおすすめを聞くとき

naturalUsage.before: somewhere nearby で場所の種類を限定せずおすすめを尋ねられます。
naturalUsage.after: 食事・買い物などの目的を先に共有すると、somewhere nearby がどんな場所を指すか伝わります。

exampleDialogue.before: A: Could you recommend somewhere nearby? B: There's a nice café around the corner.
exampleDialogue.after: A: We're looking for lunch. Could you recommend somewhere nearby? B: There's a nice café around the corner.

items.title: I can't get this to work.
I think it's worth a try.

phrase.before: In my opinion, it's worth trying.
phrase.after: I think it's worth a try.

japanese.before: 私の意見では、試す価値があります。
japanese.after: 試してみる価値はあると思います。

naturalUsage.before: 意見であることを示してから、worth + 動名詞で価値を伝えます。
naturalUsage.after: I think で意見をやわらかく伝えます。worth a try は、結果は分からなくても試す価値があるという自然な会話表現です。

exampleDialogue.before: A: Should we use the new app? B: In my opinion, it's worth trying.
exampleDialogue.after: A: Should we use the new app? B: I think it's worth a try.

commonMistake.before: worth to try ではなく、worth trying とします。
commonMistake.after: worth a try と worth trying はどちらも自然です。worth to try とは言いません。

items.title: Why don't we start with the easiest part?
We could give it another day.
That seems like the best option.
Could you say that another way?
Let me make sure I understood.

exampleDialogue.before: A: Send the draft by noon. B: Let me make sure I understood. You need it before lunch, right?
exampleDialogue.after: A: Send the draft by noon. B: Let me make sure I understood. You need it by twelve, right?

items.title: I didn't catch the last part.
I'll get back to you by Friday.
Could we move the meeting to three?

commonMistake.before: I'm running late は明確な遅刻、running behind は予定からの遅れを広く表します。
commonMistake.after: running late も running behind も、予定より遅れているときに使えます。状況が不明なら behind schedule と補えます。

commonMistake.before: divide the work equally も可能ですが、人ごとの量には evenly が自然です。
commonMistake.after: evenly と equally は、どちらも作業量を均等に分ける意味で使えます。divide のあとに the work を置きます。

items.title: It was thoughtful of you to ask.
I didn't mean to leave you out.
I'm afraid this isn't what I ordered.
Would it be possible to exchange this?
There seems to be an extra charge.
Thank you for sorting that out.
You won't believe what happened next.
It turned out to be a misunderstanding.
I'm working on being more consistent.
I've made more progress than I realized.
I'm taking it one step at a time.

commonMistake.before: step by step も使えますが、この文では one step at a time が自然です。
commonMistake.after: one step at a time は一度に一歩ずつ進める意味です。take it step by step も自然な表現です。

items.title: What would you like to improve next?
I understand your point, but I see it differently.
I'm not sure that's the whole picture.
Let's agree to disagree on that.

naturalUsage.before: 互いの立場を変えずに、対立を長引かせないための表現です。
naturalUsage.after: 好みなど、結論を一つにする必要がない話題で使います。共同の決定が必要な場面では、次の解決策も話し合いましょう。

items.title: Let me walk you through the main idea.
The key takeaway is that small changes add up.
I'd like to build on that idea.
Does anyone have a different perspective?
What would a fair compromise look like?
I can be flexible on the timing.
That works for me, provided we keep the scope small.

naturalUsage.before: provided ... で、合意に必要な条件を明確に示します。
naturalUsage.after: provided (that) ... は条件付きの合意を示す、少し改まった表現です。日常会話なら as long as ... も自然です。

items.title: I think we're closer to an agreement.
I'm still getting the hang of it.
That idea is worth keeping in mind.
We're on the same page now.

commonMistake.before: 実際に同じページを開いている意味だけではなく、認識の一致にも使います。
commonMistake.after: 意味は「共通の理解がある」です。We are in the same page. ではなく on the same page と言います。

items.title: Just to keep you in the loop, the deadline has changed.
Could you clarify what you need from me?
I'll make sure this is handled today.
I appreciate you bringing this to my attention.
Looking back, I would have approached it differently.

japanese.before: 振り返ると、今なら別のやり方で取り組むと思います。
japanese.after: 振り返ると、別のやり方で取り組めばよかったと思います。

exampleDialogue.before: A: Would you run the project the same way again? B: Looking back, I would have approached it differently.
exampleDialogue.after: A: Now that you've seen the results, would you have made the same choices? B: Looking back, I would have approached it differently.

items.title: The experience changed how I think about success.
There isn't always a clear-cut answer.
What matters most is how we respond.
I can see both sides of the argument.
The issue is more subtle than it first appears.
I wouldn't go so far as to say that.
To put it another way, we're treating the symptom, not the cause.

commonMistake.before: put it in another way も通じますが、定型表現は put it another way です。
commonMistake.after: To put it another way は言い換えの合図です。put の目的語 it を落とさず、put it another way とまとめて使います。

items.title: I don't have a firm view on that yet.

naturalUsage.before: 無知ではなく、判断を保留していることを落ち着いて伝えます。
naturalUsage.after: yet を添えて、今は判断を保留しているが、今後考えがまとまる可能性を示します。

commonMistake.before: I have no opinion. は関心がないようにも響くため、この表現はより慎重です。
commonMistake.after: I have no opinion. も正しい表現です。この文の firm view は「考えが固まった意見」を表します。

items.title: That raises a broader question about who benefits.
We may need to rethink the assumptions behind our plan.

items.title: L and r, plus c, k, j, z, y, x, and q

phonicsTarget.before: Remaining common alphabet sounds: c, k, j, z, y, x, q
phonicsTarget.after: L and r, plus c, k, j, z, y, x, and q

japaneseHint.before: cはcatでは/k/、jは/dʒ/、yはyesの短い子音です。xは多くの場合/k/と/s/を続けます。
japaneseHint.after: lは舌先を上の歯ぐきにつけ、rでは舌を後ろへ引いて上につけません。cはcatでは/k/、xはboxでは/ks/、qはquizでは/kw/です。

mouthTip.before: Use the back of the tongue for /k/. Round the lips while starting /kw/. Keep /ks/ together at the end of a word.
mouthTip.after: For /l/, touch the ridge behind the upper teeth with the tongue tip. For /r/, raise or bunch the tongue without touching the roof. Use the back of the tongue for /k/ and keep final /ks/ together.

practiceSentence.after: Look right at the red fox.

audioFocus.after: Listen to light and right. Then try the other first and last sounds.
Listen to the short vowel in cat.
Listen to the short vowel in sit.
Listen to the vowel in hot. Notice how each accent sounds.
Listen to the short vowel in bed.
Listen to the short vowel in sun.

items.title: CVC blending and clear final consonants

mouthTip.before: Stretch the first two sounds just enough to connect them, then stop cleanly on the final consonant.
mouthTip.after: Join the first consonant to the vowel, then finish with the last consonant. Do not add a vowel after it.

audioFocus.after: Join the sounds into a word. Listen for the final consonant.
Listen to both consonants at the start of blue.
Listen to both consonants at the start of brown.
Keep the first consonants together. Listen to spin and street.
Listen to ship and chip. The start of chip has a short stop.

practiceSentence.after: Those three things are over there.

audioFocus.after: Listen to think and this. Your voice starts in this.
Listen to when, phone, and sing. Keep the end of sing smooth.

japaneseHint.before: 最後のeは読まず、その前のaを文字名の/eɪ/に変えます。
japaneseHint.after: 最後のeは読まず、その前のaを文字名の/eɪ/に変えます。 ここでの語に共通するパターンです。have・give・loveのような例外もあります。

audioFocus.after: Listen to cap, then cape. The vowel changes.

japaneseHint.before: 最後のeは無音で、iは/aɪ/になります。短いiのsitと比べます。
japaneseHint.after: 最後のeは無音で、iは/aɪ/になります。短いiのsitと比べます。 ここでの語に共通するパターンです。have・give・loveのような例外もあります。

audioFocus.after: Listen to bit, then bite. The vowel changes.

japaneseHint.before: 最後のeは読まず、oを滑らかな/oʊ/にします。hopとhopeを聞き分けます。
japaneseHint.after: 最後のeは読まず、oを滑らかな/oʊ/にします。hopとhopeを聞き分けます。 ここでの語に共通するパターンです。have・give・loveのような例外もあります。

audioFocus.after: Listen to hop, then hope. The vowel changes.

japaneseHint.after: u_eは/juː/または/uː/、e_eは/iː/になります。最後のeは発音しません。 ここでの語に共通するパターンです。have・give・loveのような例外もあります。
